title: A quiet word
text: {boss.first} has asked you into the small meeting room, the one with the glass wall and no window. There is a folder on the table with your name on it.

choices.label: Listen, and ask what good looks like

outcomes.text: {boss.first} had expected a fight. Instead we wrote three goals on one page. It felt like the first adult conversation we'd had.
I took notes. I asked for a date to review it. {boss.first} nodded slowly, as if recalibrating.
I came with my own numbers. Some were right. {boss.first} adjusted one thing and left the rest standing.
It turned into an argument. {boss.first} went quiet in a way I did not like.

choices.label: Look at other jobs that night

outcomes.text: I updated the CV before I got home. It was the most productive evening I'd had in months.
I applied to six places and heard back from one. It was a start.

title: The rumour
text: It starts in the kitchen. Someone's friend in finance has seen a spreadsheet with a column headed 'headcount'. By lunch half the floor knows, and nobody has said the word.

outcomes.text: {boss.first} said nothing was decided, in the voice of someone for whom it was. At least I knew where I stood.
{boss.first} told me, off the record, that my role was safe for now. I believed it more than I should have.
Three interviews in a fortnight. When the announcement came I already had an offer in my pocket.
Everyone else was looking too. The market was thin. I was glad I had started early.

choices.label: Keep my head down and work

outcomes.text: I stayed late for a month and said nothing. I wasn't on the list. I don't know if that was why.
It didn't help. A good quarter doesn't outweigh a bad spreadsheet.

title: Your idea, their slide
text: The deck is on the big screen and slide four is your idea. It has {co.first}'s name under it.

outcomes.text: The room went quiet. {boss.first} asked for the draft history. It had my name on it. I was right and slightly sick about it.
I said, 'I'm glad that landed.' Everybody understood. {co.first} did not look up for the rest of the hour.
{co.first} apologised and meant it, mostly. The next deck had my name where it belonged.
{co.first} said they'd 'misremembered'. It was a lie we both agreed to accept.

choices.label: Let it go, and keep better records

outcomes.text: From then on everything I wrote was dated and sent to the whole team. It worked. It also felt a little joyless.
I let it go. I did not forget it. The next time it happened I was ready.

title: Drinks on the firm
text: A promotion lands and so does the invitation: Thursday, the bar by the station, everybody expected. People who haven't spoken to you in a year are suddenly delighted.

outcomes.text: I stood the first round and made a short speech I'd rehearsed in the shower. It went down well. The bill did not.
A good night. Somebody told me, in confidence, what the last person in the job had been paid. I'm glad I know.
One drink, one toast, one exit before the singing. Exactly right.
I left early and was told I was 'quiet now you're senior'. I wasn't, I was tired.
I went home. The next morning I heard everything I'd missed, and some of it was about me.
I had the evening to myself. It was lovely, and cost me a little capital I didn't know I'd spent.

title: The vote
text: The union has called a vote on action over pay and conditions. The leaflet in your pigeonhole says every voice matters. The notice on the wall says the opposite.

outcomes.text: The stoppage lasted nine days. We won most of it. The first payslip afterwards was lighter than I'd like and the mood on the floor was electric.
It dragged to three weeks and ended in a fudge. I'm proud of it and I'm still paying it off.
The motion carried without me. People remembered who had voted which way, quietly, for a long time.
The strike failed to get a majority. I'd like to think I helped. A few colleagues stopped saying hello.

choices.label: Abstain, and stay out of it

outcomes.text: Nobody could blame me for either. Nobody could thank me either.
I took the day as leave. The picket line was all anyone talked about on my return.

title: Working from home
text: Management has announced a hybrid policy, two days in the office, three at home, 'subject to review'. Your commute looks different tonight.

outcomes.text: No commute, no small talk, and by March I had a routine I loved and a face the team hardly recognised.
I got more done than I ever had, at the kitchen table, in a jumper. The team noticed. So did the boss.

choices.label: Go in more than I have to

outcomes.text: The office was empty and I enjoyed it. I was seen, which in practice counts for something.
I kept up the old routine. It was good for the friendships and bad for the budget.

choices.label: Argue for four days at home

outcomes.text: They said no, politely. I got a cushion on my chair and a half-day on Fridays.
They said yes to a trial. I made it work. Three of my colleagues asked how.

title: A training budget
text: HR has sent a note: everyone has money to spend on 'development' before the end of the quarter. Nobody is quite sure how.

outcomes.text: Six evenings over eight weeks and a certificate. I learned more than I expected and it showed in March.
The course was dull but the person next to me knew someone. A job interview followed.
Two days, fourteen badges, and one conversation that mattered. I flew home with a plan.
I spent most of it in the hotel bar. Nobody asked what I'd learned, which was lucky.

choices.label: Spend it on books and tools

outcomes.text: A shelf of books and a good chair. The chair did more for my work than the books.
I bought a very good monitor. I am not ashamed.

title: Someone takes an interest
text: A senior person, who has never said more to you than hello in the lift, asks if you'd like a coffee. 'Nothing formal,' they say. It sounds formal.

outcomes.text: It turned into a monthly habit. They told me the unwritten rules of the place, and one or two of the written ones.
It was awkward for the first few meetings and enormously useful for the next fifty.

choices.label: Ask what they want from it

outcomes.text: They laughed. 'To see someone do it better than I did.' I thought about that for a long time.
They wanted a favour, eventually. A small one. It was still a favour.
They nodded and said the door was open. It is never as open the second time.
I was too busy. I was always too busy.

title: Sunday dread
text: It starts on Sunday afternoon now: a tightness in the chest, a list that grows while you look at it. Last week you cried in the stationery cupboard and told no one.

outcomes.text: {boss.first} did something I hadn't expected: listened, took two projects off me and sent me home early. I felt guilty and slept for ten hours.
{boss.first} said all the right words and changed nothing. At least I'd said it aloud.
Two weeks, no email. By day five I was bored. By day ten I was myself.
The leave was approved and ruined by a handover that wouldn't stay handed over.
I pushed through. The work held up, and a few months later, something else did not.
It got worse. I was lucky someone noticed before I did anything I'd regret.

title: Across the open plan
text: The person from the other team keeps appearing at the printer when you do. Their laugh carries. Everyone has noticed, which makes noticing impossible.

outcomes.text: A very ordinary lunch and a very good afternoon. We agreed to keep it quiet; it lasted about a week.
They said yes, then no, then yes. By the time it settled I was invested.
We remained very good colleagues. Years later I'd think about that.
I played it safe. They moved to another office six months later and the printer was quiet.
There was a form. There was always a form. We filled it in together and laughed at question six.
The policy was clear. It would have meant one of us leaving. We were both sensible, and a little sad.

title: A move for the job
text: The firm is closing your office. Two options: a transfer to the head office four hundred miles away, or a redundancy package with some strings in it.

outcomes.text: A new city, a new flat, a team that did not know me. The first six months were hard. After that it started to feel like mine.
I hated it for a year and loved it for ten. I'm glad I went.
The money gave me a year to think. I thought about it a lot, and I spent it carefully.
The package was less than they'd implied. It paid for two months. The rest I did myself.
They said they'd consider it. Eight weeks later they said yes, on a trial basis. I was the only one in the building who still had a desk at home.
The answer was no. I'd lost two months to asking.

title: A little something on the side
text: A friend needs a thing done that is half your job and half a favour. The pay is cash. The contract says you can't take outside work.

outcomes.text: It was easy money and a small thrill. Nobody ever found out. I did it again twice.
My manager found out two months later. 'We'll say no more about it,' she said, which meant plenty.
They said yes, with conditions, and a nod. I liked the honesty and I liked the money.
They said no, and thanked me for asking. My friend found someone else.
My friend sulked. Years later it came up and we both laughed.
I felt like a saint and a mug in equal parts.
